paras: The Rocheport disturbance of 1882 was a night of conflict in Rocheport, Missouri, on April 1, 1882, in which an officer fired at a Black man, Wm. Barber, and a volley from an alley later wounded several white men. No one was reported killed, about ten Black men were arrested, and seven of them were later taken to the state penitentiary. The wire carried the story across the country as a race riot, under headlines such as "Colored Rioters in Missouri" and "War of Races."

According to the fullest account, printed in the Grenada Sentinel, trouble began when Jos. Mitchell, described as "colored," was said to have "insulted" Marion Wyatt, a white man, and was knocked down when he tried to strike him. A man named General Wilhite and several other Black men sided with Mitchell, and Wyatt drew a revolver. The Black men then gathered, about twenty-five strong, in the street opposite the post office; the wire report called them "drunken negroes" who had assaulted white men.

Special deputies were sworn in and told the crowd to scatter or be arrested. When Wm. Barber tried to strike officer Thos. White, the Sentinel said, White shot at him twice "in self-defence" but missed in the darkness. The crowd fled, and some of its members were taken into custody.

About twenty minutes later, as fifteen or twenty white men and boys stood at the door of Chambers Bros. & Co.'s dry-goods store, a volley of gunfire came from an alley across the street, which the reports attributed to Black men. The store front was riddled, and the Sentinel named eight wounded men, including Marion Wyatt; the wire said none was hurt seriously.

About ten Black men were arrested and locked up that night. In May the Mexico Weekly Ledger reported that Sheriff Stone of Boone County had passed through Mexico with thirteen Black prisoners bound for the penitentiary, seven of whom it said had been in "the late riot at Rocheport." The coverage names no charges, trial or sentences, and no inquiry into the officer's shooting appears in it.

By late June the town had passed an ordinance under which vagrants were to be jailed and then hired out publicly for four months to the highest bidder, and the Richmond Democrat linked the measure to the night when "colored mokes shot into a crowd of citizens."

The story reached the press as a St. Louis Republican special, which the Evening Star, the Lancaster Intelligencer, the Las Vegas Gazette, the Cheyenne Leader and the Portland Daily Press printed on April 3 and 4. Headlines included "Riotous Negroes" and "War of Races at Rocheport, Mo.," and the Lancaster paper called those arrested "ruffians." All the versions told the story from the side of the deputies and the white townspeople, presenting the officer's shots as a response to an "assailant" and treating the Black crowd as the aggressor.

Briefs in smaller papers inflated the event: the Iron County Register said a mob of Black men had "wantonly killed eight young white men," and the Weekly Clarion said eight men were shot. Later Missouri items referred to the prisoners as "coons" and to the shooters as "mokes."

Reports disagreed on the date, with the wire and the Sentinel giving Saturday night, April 1, and later briefs giving "the 2d" or Sunday evening. They also differed on casualties: one copy of the Republican special said one man was wounded, most said eight wounded, and the Iron County Register alone said eight were killed. One copy also printed the town's name as "Rockport," while the other reports and the Boone County sheriff's role point to Rocheport.

reader.title: Rocheport disturbance of 1882
bases: The only violence directed at a named Black person was a special-deputy officer firing twice at Wm. Barber while dispersing a crowd of Black men (A7, A3, A1); the larger shooting in the episode was by Black men at white men, followed by mass arrests (A1, A9).

The St. Louis Republican special (A3, A1) and the differently worded, more detailed Grenada Sentinel account (A7) agree that an officer fired at and missed a Black man trying to strike him, and the Mexico Ledger confirms the 'riot' and its prisoners (A9); all accounts come from the officers' and white residents' side.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republican special (wire)
accounts.gist: Twenty or more drunken Black men made a disturbance and assaulted white men; a deputy fired at one who tried to strike him and missed; later a volley from an alley wounded one (A3) or eight (A1), none seriously; ten were arrested.

accounts.label: Rocheport narrative (Grenada Sentinel)
accounts.gist: A quarrel in which Jos. Mitchell 'insulted' Marion Wyatt drew a crowd of twenty-five Black men; officer Thos. White fired twice at Wm. Barber in 'self-defence' and missed; twenty minutes later a volley from an alley wounded eight named white men.

accounts.label: Iron County Register brief
accounts.gist: A mob of drunken Black men rode into Rocheport on Sunday evening and killed eight young white men.

framing.detail: Wire copies ran under 'Riotous Negroes', 'Colored Rioters in Missouri' and 'War of Races at Rocheport', calling the crowd 'drunken negroes' and the officer's shot a response to an 'assailant'.
The Grenada Sentinel said officer White shot 'in self-defence' and called Wyatt 'as quiet and peaceable a man as can be found'.
Missouri papers called the prisoners 'coons' and the shooters 'colored mokes', and one held up the town's vagrancy ordinance as a model.

conflicts.note: The dated Rocheport account and the wire both put it on Saturday night, April 1; the later briefs likely confused the dispatch date.
The Sentinel names eight wounded, supporting the wire's eight; the Register's 'killed' is contradicted by every other report.
Only one wire copy prints Rockport; the follow-ups and the Boone County sheriff's role point to Rocheport.
